paper_context.research_question: How can one build effective named entity recognition (NER) systems for new languages without human annotation in the target language, given a well-trained NER system in a source language (English)?
contribution_type: heuristic data selection scheme for annotation projection
representation projection approach for direct NER model transfer
co-decoding schemes combining multiple projection-based systems
contribution_style: practical engineering of weak supervision techniques
combination of existing methods (annotation projection, embedding mapping) with novel selection and fusion strategies
empirical validation across multiple language pairs
main_claims: A frequency-based heuristic data selection scheme can effectively filter noisy projection-labeled NER data from comparable corpora, improving target-language NER accuracy especially when alignment quality is low
Cross-lingual word embedding projection enables direct transfer of English NER models to target languages without retraining, by mapping target-language embeddings into English vector space
Rank-based co-decoding that prioritizes high-precision annotation projection outputs while adding balanced-recall representation projection outputs outperforms individual projection approaches

Combined weakly supervised systems achieve competitive performance relative to supervised baselines and outperform prior cross-lingual NER methods (Täckström et al. 2012, Tsai et al. 2016) on CoNLL benchmarks
expected_evaluation_dimensions: F1 score, precision, and recall on in-house NER test sets (Japanese, Korean, German, Portuguese with 50+ entity types)
F1 score on CoNLL 02/03 development and test sets (Spanish, Dutch, German with 4 entity types)
Comparison against supervised learning baselines trained on target-language annotated data
Comparison against prior cross-lingual NER approaches (Täckström et al. 2012, Tsai et al. 2016)
Ablation analysis: impact of data selection thresholds (q, n) on training data size and performance
Analysis of precision-recall tradeoffs between annotation projection (high precision, low recall) and representation projection (balanced)
Effectiveness of co-decoding schemes (confidence-based vs. rank-based) across different language pairs

extracted_claims.claim_label: Data selection improves annotation projection under low alignment quality
extracted_claims.claim_text: A frequency-based heuristic data selection scheme can effectively filter noisy projection-labeled NER data from comparable corpora, improving target-language NER accuracy especially when alignment quality is low.
evidence: Section 3.1 introduces frequency-based quality metric q(y) and entity count threshold n(y) for selecting projection-labeled sentences
Table 2 shows +13.9 F1 for Japanese (alignment F1: 69.4) and +20.0 F1 for Korean (alignment F1: 62.0) with data selection
Table 2 shows smaller improvements for German (+0.7 F1, alignment F1: 76.1) and Portuguese (+1.2 F1, alignment F1: 88.0) with higher alignment quality

Section 3.2 explicitly states: 'When the alignment accuracy is low (e.g., as for Japanese and Korean) and hence the projection-labeled NER data are quite noisy, the proposed data selection scheme is very effective'
uncertainty_flags: Threshold parameters (q, n) are tuned per language; generalization of optimal thresholds across languages not demonstrated
Frequency-based reliability assumption (Section 3.1) relies on independence of English NER and alignment systems; actual error correlation not empirically validated
No ablation study isolating the contribution of quality score q(y) vs. entity count n(y) thresholds
Test sets are in-house (30K–45K tokens); generalization to other domains/corpora unclear

extracted_claims.claim_label: Representation projection enables direct NER model transfer without retraining
extracted_claims.claim_text: Cross-lingual word embedding projection enables direct transfer of English NER models to target languages without retraining, by mapping target-language embeddings into English vector space.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes weighted least-squares linear mapping M_f^e from target language embeddings to English space (Eq. 7)
Section 4.3 states: 'Model transfer is achieved simply by projecting the target language word embeddings into the English vector space and decoding these using the English NER system'
Table 3 shows representation projection (NN1, NN2) produces F1 scores of 48.4–64.9 across four languages without target-language model retraining
Section 4.1 specifies 300-dim embeddings for English, 800-dim for target languages, trained with word2vec variant
uncertainty_flags: Linear mapping assumption (Eq. 7) may not hold across typologically distant language pairs; no analysis of mapping quality or language-pair similarity effects
Dictionary size fixed at ~5K–6K word pairs; sensitivity to dictionary size and quality not systematically explored
Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) handling (Section 4.3) uses English embeddings or NER-trained unk vector; impact on performance not quantified
Embedding dimensionality differs between source (300) and target (800); justification and impact on mapping quality not discussed
No direct comparison of representation projection performance vs. annotation projection on same language pairs with controlled conditions

extracted_claims.claim_label: Rank-based co-decoding outperforms individual projection approaches
extracted_claims.claim_text: Rank-based co-decoding that prioritizes high-precision annotation projection outputs while adding balanced-recall representation projection outputs outperforms individual projection approaches.
evidence: Section 5 describes rank-based scheme: 'first include all the entities detected by the annotation projection system. Then, it will add all the entities detected by the representation projection system that do not conflict'
Table 3 shows rank-based co-decoding (AP+NN2) achieves highest F1 among weakly supervised for Korean (51.8), German (69.3), Portuguese (69.9); second-highest for Japanese (59.3)
Table 3 reports improvements of 2.9–6.2 F1 over best individual system
Table 4 shows confidence-based co-decoding (AP+NN1) achieves highest F1 for Spanish (63.4) and Dutch (66.7) on CoNLL dev data
uncertainty_flags: Rank-based scheme prioritizes AP due to observed high precision; this heuristic is not formally justified or optimized
Conflict definition (footnote 3) is binary (overlap or tag mismatch); no soft conflict resolution or weighted combination explored
Co-decoding scheme selection differs between in-house (rank-based) and CoNLL (confidence-based) data; no principled method for choosing scheme per dataset
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided for F1 improvements
Ablation study missing: impact of conflict resolution strategy, entity boundary overlap tolerance, and tag mismatch handling not isolated

extracted_claims.claim_label: Combined systems outperform prior cross-lingual NER methods
extracted_claims.claim_text: Combined weakly supervised systems achieve competitive performance relative to supervised baselines and outperform prior cross-lingual NER methods (Täckström et al. 2012, Tsai et al. 2016) on CoNLL benchmarks.
evidence: Table 5 (referenced in Section 6.3) compares top systems against Täckström et al. (2012) and Tsai et al. (2016) on CoNLL test data
Section 6.3 states: 'Our systems outperform the previous two approaches, especially for German, and are closer to supervised learning'

Section 1 (lines 196–199) claims: 'The results show that the combined systems outperform the state-of-the-art cross-lingual NER approaches proposed in Täckström et al. (2012) and Tsai et al. (2016) on the CoNLL NER test data'
uncertainty_flags: Table 5 is referenced but not provided in manuscript excerpt; specific F1 scores and margins vs. prior work cannot be verified from provided text
Comparison is limited to two prior methods; broader landscape of cross-lingual NER approaches not surveyed
Supervised baselines use different training data sizes (90K–272K tokens); fair comparison requires controlling for training data size
No error analysis or qualitative comparison of failure modes between proposed and prior methods
CoNLL evaluation uses only 4 entity types; in-house evaluation uses 50+ types; generalization across entity type granularity unclear

extracted_claims.claim_label: Annotation projection has high precision, representation projection has balanced precision-recall
extracted_claims.claim_text: The annotation projection system tends to have high precision and low recall, while the representation projection system tends to have more balanced precision and recall.
evidence: Section 5 states: 'the annotation projection system tends to have a high precision and low recall, i.e., it detects few entities, but for the detected entities the accuracy is high. The representation projection system tends to have a more balanced precision and recall'
Table 3 shows AP precision/recall: Japanese (71.3/44.7), Korean (69.3/26.9), German (77.6/58.0), Portuguese (84.4/50.1)
Table 3 shows NN2 precision/recall: Japanese (59.9/42.4), Korean (59.3/37.1), German (63.7/66.1), Portuguese (66.0/63.4)
NN2 shows more balanced P/R across languages compared to AP
uncertainty_flags: Precision-recall tradeoff is observed empirically but not explained mechanistically; why AP favors precision and NN2 favors recall is not analyzed
NN1 vs. NN2 comparison shows NN2 has lower precision but higher recall; smoothing layer effect (Section 2.2) not isolated or ablated
Observation is based on in-house data; CoNLL results (Table 4) show different patterns (NN1 has high precision for Spanish/Dutch), suggesting dataset-dependent behavior
No analysis of how precision-recall tradeoff varies with alignment quality, embedding quality, or other system parameters

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Frequency of entity-tag pairs in projection-labeled data is a reliable proxy for annotation correctness, because English NER and alignment systems are independent and unlikely to make consistent errors simultaneously.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.1 states: 'The intuition is that if an entity e is labeled by a tag l with higher frequency than other tags in the projection-labeled data, it is more likely that the annotation is correct, because the source (English) NER system and the alignment system are independent statistical models and it is less likely that both systems make consistent errors simultaneously generating the same wrong tag.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If English NER and alignment errors are correlated (e.g., both systems systematically misclassify certain entity types or language phenomena), frequency-based filtering will fail to remove noisy labels and may even amplify systematic biases. This would undermine the effectiveness of the data selection scheme.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Linear mapping in embedding space (Eq. 7) is sufficient to align target-language embeddings with English embeddings for NER task.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2 formulates cross-lingual mapping as weighted least-squares: M_f^e = arg min_M Σ w_i ||u_i - M v_i||^2
Section 4.4 notes: 'we opt for the first solution in this paper because of its flexibility: we can map all languages to English rather than requiring separate embeddings for each language pair'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If embedding spaces have non-linear structure or language-specific geometric properties, linear mapping will introduce systematic distortions. This could degrade representation projection performance, especially for typologically distant language pairs or languages with different morphological complexity.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Dictionary size of ~5K–6K word pairs is optimal for cross-lingual embedding mapping; larger dictionaries harm performance.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2 states: 'To control the size of the dictionary, we only include word pairs with a minimum frequency threshold. We set the threshold to obtain approximately 5K to 6K unique word pairs for a target language, as experiments show that larger dictionaries might harm the performance of representation projection for direct NER model transfer.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If dictionary size is suboptimal, mapping quality degrades. The claim that larger dictionaries harm performance is stated without evidence or ablation study; if this is incorrect, using smaller dictionaries may unnecessarily limit mapping coverage and accuracy.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Rank-based co-decoding scheme (prioritizing AP, then adding non-conflicting RP entities) is superior to confidence-based schemes across all datasets.
supporting_evidence: Section 5 develops rank-based scheme based on observed precision-recall tradeoffs
Table 3 shows rank-based co-decoding achieves best F1 for 3 of 4 in-house languages
Table 4 shows confidence-based co-decoding achieves best F1 for 2 of 3 CoNLL languages
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The choice of co-decoding scheme is dataset-dependent (rank-based for in-house, confidence-based for CoNLL). If the assumption that rank-based is universally superior is incorrect, the method lacks robustness and requires dataset-specific tuning, reducing practical applicability.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Comparable corpora with word alignment are available for target languages; alignment quality is the primary factor affecting annotation projection performance.
supporting_evidence: Section 3 states: 'we develop a heuristic scheme that can effectively select good-quality projection-labeled NER data from noisy comparable corpora (not necessarily parallel corpora)'
Section 3.2 provides alignment F1 scores for each language and correlates them with data selection improvements
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If comparable corpora or alignment tools are unavailable for a target language, annotation projection cannot be applied. The method's applicability is limited to language pairs with existing alignment resources. Robustness to poor alignment quality is claimed but not systematically tested across a range of alignment F1 scores.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: English NER system trained on newswire data (320K tokens) generalizes to target-language text from comparable corpora without domain adaptation.
supporting_evidence: Section 6.2 states: 'the source (English) NER system is a linear-chain CRF model trained with 320K tokens of human-annotated English newswire data'
Section 6.3 states: 'the source (English) NER system for annotation projection is a linear-chain CRF model trained with the CoNLL English training data (~200K tokens)'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If target-language comparable corpora have different domain, genre, or entity distribution than English newswire, the English NER system's predictions will be noisy, degrading annotation projection quality. Domain mismatch is not analyzed or controlled for.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Word embeddings trained on monolingual data (word2vec variant) capture sufficient semantic and syntactic information for NER without language-specific features (gazetteers, character-level representations).
supporting_evidence: Section 2.2 states: 'We do not employ other common features such as gazetteers or character-level representations as such features might not be readily available or might not transfer to other languages.'
Section 4.1 describes monolingual word2vec training with distance-weighted context
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If language-specific features (gazetteers, morphological analyzers, character-level models) are necessary for NER in target languages, representation projection will underperform. The assumption trades off feature richness for cross-lingual transferability; the tradeoff is not quantified.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Test sets (in-house: 30K–45K tokens; CoNLL: 35K–70K tokens) are representative of target-language NER performance and sufficient for reliable F1 estimation.
supporting_evidence: Section 6.1 describes test set sizes: 'The sizes of test data sets are ranging from 30K to 45K tokens' for in-house and '35K to 70K tokens' for CoNLL
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Small test sets may have high variance in F1 scores, especially for rare entity types. No confidence intervals or significance tests are provided. Generalization to other domains or test sets is unclear.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Exact phrasal match is the appropriate evaluation metric for NER; partial credit for boundary or type errors is not necessary.
supporting_evidence: Table 3 caption states: 'Precision, recall, F1 score on exact phrasal matches.'
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Exact match is strict; systems with near-correct boundaries or type confusions are penalized equally. If partial credit is more appropriate for downstream applications, F1 scores may not reflect practical utility. No analysis of boundary vs. type errors is provided.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Supervised baselines trained on target-language annotated data (90K–272K tokens) are valid upper-bound comparisons for weakly supervised approaches.
supporting_evidence: Section 6.2 states: 'We also provide the performance of supervised learning where the NER system is trained with human-annotated NER data in the target language (with size shown in the bracket).'
Table 3 includes supervised baseline F1 scores for each language
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Supervised baselines use different model architectures (MEMM for annotation projection, neural networks for representation projection) and different training data sizes. Fair comparison requires controlling for model and data size. The gap between weakly supervised and supervised may reflect architectural differences rather than the fundamental limitation of weak supervision.

argument_focus: Weakly supervised cross-lingual NER is feasible without target-language human annotation by combining annotation projection and representation projection approaches.
Annotation projection quality depends critically on alignment accuracy; heuristic data selection based on entity-tag frequency can filter noisy labels when alignment is poor.
Representation projection via linear embedding mapping enables direct model transfer without retraining, offering flexibility for adding new languages.
Combining high-precision annotation projection with balanced-recall representation projection via co-decoding outperforms individual approaches.
Proposed methods outperform prior cross-lingual NER work (Täckström et al. 2012, Tsai et al. 2016) on CoNLL benchmarks while remaining significantly below supervised performance.

Representation projection approach: linear mapping of target-language embeddings to English vector space for direct NER model transfer without retraining.
Co-decoding schemes: confidence-based and rank-based methods to combine annotation projection and representation projection outputs.

Analysis of precision-recall tradeoffs between annotation projection (high precision, low recall) and representation projection (balanced) (Table 3).
Effectiveness of co-decoding schemes (confidence-based vs. rank-based) across different language pairs and datasets (Tables 3, 4).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This methodological paper presents a coherent three-part approach to weakly supervised cross-lingual NER: (1) annotation projection with heuristic data selection (Section 3), (2) representation projection via embedding mapping (Section 4), and (3) co-decoding schemes combining both approaches (Section 5). The logical flow is generally sound: the paper identifies a practical problem (building NER for new languages without target-language annotation), proposes two complementary solutions addressing different failure modes (annotation projection struggles with alignment noise; representation projection lacks recall), and combines them to mitigate individual weaknesses. However, the argument structure exhibits critical gaps in mechanistic explanation, assumption validation, and methodological justification. The frequency-based reliability assumption (A1) underpins the entire data selection scheme but lacks empirical validation of error independence. The linear embedding mapping assumption (A2) is stated without testing on typologically diverse pairs. The co-decoding scheme selection (rank-based vs. confidence-based) differs between datasets without principled justification, suggesting dataset-specific tuning rather than a generalizable method. The paper's contribution is primarily engineering-focused—combining existing techniques (annotation projection, embedding mapping, ensemble decoding)—with limited novelty in individual components. Strengths include comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple language pairs and entity type granularities, clear presentation of precision-recall tradeoffs, and practical applicability. Concerns center on unvalidated assumptions, missing ablations, lack of statistical rigor, and limited mechanistic insight into why the proposed methods work.
logical_argument_graph: Problem statement (Intro): Building NER for new languages without target-language annotation is expensive and difficult; two existing approaches (annotation projection, direct model transfer) have complementary weaknesses.
Claim C1 (Section 3): Annotation projection quality depends on alignment accuracy; frequency-based data selection can filter noisy labels when alignment is poor.
Evidence for C1: Table 2 shows +13.9 F1 (Japanese, low alignment) and +20.0 F1 (Korean, low alignment) with data selection; smaller gains for high-alignment languages (German +0.7, Portuguese +1.2).
Assumption A1 (Section 3.1): Frequency-based filtering works because English NER and alignment errors are independent; higher frequency implies correctness.

Logical gap: A1 is stated intuitively but not empirically validated; error correlation between systems not measured; assumption could fail if both systems systematically misclassify certain phenomena.
Claim C2 (Section 4): Linear embedding mapping enables direct NER model transfer without retraining; target-language embeddings projected to English space allow English NER system to decode.
Evidence for C2: Section 4.3 describes projection procedure; Table 3 shows NN1/NN2 achieve F1 48.4–64.9 without retraining.
Assumption A2 (Section 4.2): Linear mapping (Eq. 7) is sufficient for cross-lingual alignment; weighted least-squares optimization finds optimal mapping.

Logical gap: A2 assumes embedding spaces have linear structure; no analysis of mapping quality, language-pair similarity effects, or non-linear alternatives; dimensionality mismatch (300 vs. 800) not justified.
Claim C5 (Section 5): Annotation projection has high precision/low recall; representation projection has balanced precision/recall; this tradeoff motivates co-decoding.
Evidence for C5: Table 3 shows AP precision/recall (Japanese 71.3/44.7, Korean 69.3/26.9) vs. NN2 (59.9/42.4, 59.3/37.1); NN2 more balanced.
Logical gap: Tradeoff is observed empirically but not explained mechanistically; why AP favors precision and NN2 favors recall is not analyzed; smoothing layer effect (NN2) not isolated.
Claim C3 (Section 5): Rank-based co-decoding (prioritize AP, add non-conflicting RP entities) outperforms individual systems.
Evidence for C3: Table 3 shows rank-based AP+NN2 achieves highest F1 for Korean (51.8), German (69.3), Portuguese (69.9); improvements of 2.9–6.2 F1 over best individual system.
Assumption A4 (Section 5): Rank-based scheme is superior across datasets; prioritizing AP due to observed high precision is optimal.

Logical gap: Table 4 shows confidence-based co-decoding achieves best F1 for Spanish/Dutch on CoNLL data; scheme selection differs between datasets without principled method; suggests dataset-specific tuning rather than generalizable approach.
Claim C4 (Section 6.3): Combined systems outperform prior cross-lingual NER methods (Täckström et al. 2012, Tsai et al. 2016) on CoNLL test data.
Evidence for C4: Section 6.3 states 'Our systems outperform the previous two approaches, especially for German, and are closer to supervised learning'; Table 5 referenced but not provided in excerpt.

Logical gap: Table 5 not provided; specific F1 scores and margins cannot be verified; comparison limited to two prior methods; broader landscape not surveyed; supervised baselines use different training data sizes.
Conclusion (Section 7): Combined weakly supervised approach provides strong baseline for cross-lingual NER without target-language annotation.

Overall coherence: Paper follows logical progression (problem → two complementary solutions → combination → evaluation), but critical assumptions lack validation, mechanistic explanations are sparse, and methodological choices (co-decoding scheme selection, threshold tuning) appear dataset-dependent rather than principled.

No error analysis or qualitative comparison of failure modes between proposed and prior methods
CoNLL evaluation uses only 4 entity types; in-house evaluation uses 50+ types; generalization across entity type granularity unclear

identified_claims.claim_label: Annotation projection has high precision, representation projection has balanced precision-recall
identified_claims.claim_text: The annotation projection system tends to have high precision and low recall, while the representation projection system tends to have more balanced precision and recall.
evidence: Section 5 states: 'the annotation projection system tends to have a high precision and low recall, i.e., it detects few entities, but for the detected entities the accuracy is high. The representation projection system tends to have a more balanced precision and recall'
Table 3 shows AP precision/recall: Japanese (71.3/44.7), Korean (69.3/26.9), German (77.6/58.0), Portuguese (84.4/50.1)
Table 3 shows NN2 precision/recall: Japanese (59.9/42.4), Korean (59.3/37.1), German (63.7/66.1), Portuguese (66.0/63.4)
NN2 shows more balanced P/R across languages compared to AP
uncertainty_flags: Precision-recall tradeoff is observed empirically but not explained mechanistically; why AP favors precision and NN2 favors recall is not analyzed
NN1 vs. NN2 comparison shows NN2 has lower precision but higher recall; smoothing layer effect (Section 2.2) not isolated or ablated
Observation is based on in-house data; CoNLL results (Table 4) show different patterns (NN1 has high precision for Spanish/Dutch), suggesting dataset-dependent behavior
No analysis of how precision-recall tradeoff varies with alignment quality, embedding quality, or other system parameters

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple language pairs and entity type granularities
strengths.description: Paper evaluates on 6 language pairs (Japanese, Korean, German, Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch) with two different entity type sets (50+ types for in-house, 4 types for CoNLL), providing broad evidence of method applicability across diverse linguistic contexts.
evidence: Section 6.1 describes two groups of NER datasets: in-house (4 languages, 50+ entity types, 30K–45K tokens) and CoNLL (3 languages, 4 entity types, 35K–70K tokens)
Table 2 shows results for 4 languages with varying alignment quality (69.4–88.0 F1)
Table 3 shows in-house results for 4 languages with detailed precision/recall breakdown
Table 4 shows CoNLL development results for 3 languages

strengths.title: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of precision-recall tradeoff between projection approaches
strengths.description: Paper explicitly identifies that annotation projection favors precision (high precision, low recall) while representation projection favors balanced precision-recall. This observation is well-supported by Table 3 data and motivates the co-decoding approach.
evidence: Section 5 clearly states the tradeoff: 'the annotation projection system tends to have a high precision and low recall... The representation projection system tends to have a more balanced precision and recall'
Table 3 provides detailed precision/recall numbers for all languages and approaches, showing consistent pattern: AP has high P, low R; NN2 has more balanced P/R

strengths.title: Practical engineering of weak supervision techniques with clear applicability
strengths.description: Paper combines existing techniques (annotation projection, embedding mapping, ensemble decoding) in a practical way that addresses real constraints: no target-language annotation, available comparable corpora, and existing source-language NER systems.
evidence: Section 3 develops heuristic data selection scheme using frequency-based quality metric; simple to implement and tune
Section 4 applies standard cross-lingual embedding mapping (Mikolov et al. 2013b) with weighted least-squares optimization
Section 5 designs two co-decoding schemes (confidence-based and rank-based) that are straightforward to implement
Paper provides sufficient implementation details (thresholds, model architectures, training procedures) for reproducibility

strengths.title: Effective data selection scheme shows substantial improvements under low alignment quality
strengths.description: Data selection scheme (Section 3.1) demonstrates strong empirical results when alignment quality is poor: +13.9 F1 for Japanese (alignment F1 69.4) and +20.0 F1 for Korean (alignment F1 62.0). This addresses a real practical problem where annotation projection is most needed but least reliable.
evidence: Table 2 shows improvements inversely correlated with alignment quality: largest gains for low-alignment languages (Japanese +13.9, Korean +20.0), smallest for high-alignment languages (German +0.7, Portuguese +1.2)

Section 3.2 explicitly states: 'When the alignment accuracy is low (e.g., as for Japanese and Korean) and hence the projection-labeled NER data are quite noisy, the proposed data selection scheme is very effective'
Alignment F1 scores provided for each language, enabling analysis of alignment quality impact

strengths.title: Co-decoding approach achieves consistent improvements over individual projection systems
strengths.description: Both co-decoding schemes (confidence-based and rank-based) improve over best individual system across all language pairs. Improvements range 1.3–6.2 F1 on in-house data and 1.3–3.6 F1 on CoNLL data, demonstrating complementarity of the two projection approaches.
evidence: Table 3 shows rank-based co-decoding improvements: Japanese +3.6 F1 (AP 55.0 → AP+NN2 59.3), Korean +6.2 F1 (NN2 45.6 → AP+NN2 51.8), German +2.9 F1 (NN2 64.9 → AP+NN2 69.3), Portuguese +5.2 F1 (NN2 64.7 → AP+NN2 69.9)
Table 4 shows confidence-based co-decoding improvements: Spanish +1.3 F1 (NN1 57.4 → AP+NN1 63.4), Dutch +1.3 F1 (AP 65.4 → AP+NN1 66.7), German +1.3 F1 (NN1 54.4 → AP+NN1 63.7)
Improvements are consistent across languages, suggesting co-decoding is a robust technique

concerns.title: Frequency-based reliability assumption lacks empirical validation
concerns.description: Section 3.1 assumes that frequency of entity-tag pairs in projection-labeled data is a reliable proxy for correctness because English NER and alignment systems are independent. However, this assumption is not empirically validated. If English NER and alignment errors are correlated, frequency-based filtering will fail to remove noisy labels and may amplify systematic biases.
evidence: Section 3.1 states: 'The intuition is that if an entity e is labeled by a tag l with higher frequency than other tags in the projection-labeled data, it is more likely that the annotation is correct, because the source (English) NER system and the alignment system are independent statistical models and it is less likely that both systems make consistent errors simultaneously generating the same wrong tag.'
No empirical analysis of error correlation between English NER and alignment systems provided
No ablation study showing that frequency-based filtering removes errors more effectively than random filtering or other baselines
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct error analysis on a sample of projection-labeled data: (1) manually annotate subset of projection-labeled sentences; (2) analyze which errors are removed by data selection vs. which persist; (3) measure correlation between English NER errors and alignment errors on same sentence pairs; (4) compare frequency-based filtering with alternative filtering schemes to isolate contribution of frequency-based approach.

concerns.title: Data selection thresholds are tuned per language without principled method or generalization analysis
concerns.description: Section 3.1 introduces two threshold parameters (q, n) for data selection. Table 2 shows different optimal thresholds for each language. No principled method for selecting thresholds is provided, and no analysis of how thresholds generalize across languages, domains, or entity type granularities.
evidence: Section 3.1 states: 'We can tune the two parameters to make tradeoffs among the annotation quality of the selected sentences, the annotation information contained in the selected sentences, and the total number of sentence selected.'
Table 2 shows different optimal (q, n) for each language; no explanation for why thresholds differ
No sensitivity analysis showing F1 as function of (q, n) thresholds; no guidance for practitioners on threshold selection for new languages
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide sensitivity analysis: (1) plot F1 score as function of q and n thresholds for each language; (2) identify plateau regions where F1 is robust to threshold changes; (3) analyze whether optimal thresholds correlate with alignment quality, language pair, or other properties; (4) propose principled method for threshold selection; (5) test whether thresholds learned on one language pair transfer to other pairs.

concerns.title: Linear embedding mapping assumption not validated for typologically diverse language pairs
concerns.description: Section 4.2 assumes linear mapping (Eq. 7) is sufficient for cross-lingual embedding alignment. However, no analysis of mapping quality, language-pair similarity effects, or validity of linearity assumption is provided. For typologically distant language pairs, linear mapping may introduce systematic distortions.
evidence: Section 4.2 formulates mapping as weighted least-squares: M_f^e = arg min_M Σ w_i ||u_i - M v_i||^2
No analysis of mapping quality (e.g., reconstruction error, alignment accuracy on held-out dictionary)
No comparison with non-linear mapping approaches (e.g., neural networks, kernel methods)
No analysis of how mapping quality correlates with language-pair similarity
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze mapping quality: (1) measure reconstruction error on held-out dictionary; (2) measure alignment accuracy on held-out word pairs; (3) compare linear mapping with non-linear alternatives; (4) analyze how mapping quality correlates with language-pair properties; (5) test whether mapping quality predicts NER performance.

concerns.title: Dictionary size claim lacks supporting evidence or ablation study
concerns.description: Section 4.2 claims that larger dictionaries harm representation projection performance but provides no evidence, ablation study, or analysis to support this claim. This is a critical design choice that affects mapping quality and coverage.
evidence: Section 4.2 states: 'We set the threshold to obtain approximately 5K to 6K unique word pairs for a target language, as experiments show that larger dictionaries might harm the performance of representation projection for direct NER model transfer.'
No ablation study showing F1 as function of dictionary size
No analysis of why larger dictionaries would harm performance
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation study on dictionary size: (1) train mapping with dictionaries of varying sizes (1K, 2K, 5K, 10K, 20K word pairs); (2) measure mapping quality for each dictionary size; (3) measure NER F1 for each dictionary size; (4) analyze why larger dictionaries might harm performance; (5) provide guidance for practitioners on optimal dictionary size.

concerns.title: Co-decoding scheme selection differs between datasets without principled justification
concerns.description: Section 5 develops two co-decoding schemes (confidence-based and rank-based). Table 3 shows rank-based co-decoding achieves best F1 for in-house data (3 of 4 languages). Table 4 shows confidence-based co-decoding achieves best F1 for CoNLL data (2 of 3 languages). No principled method for selecting scheme per dataset is provided.
evidence: Section 5 describes both schemes but does not provide principled method for choosing between them
Table 3 shows rank-based co-decoding (AP+NN2) achieves highest F1 for Korean (51.8), German (69.3), Portuguese (69.9); second-highest for Japanese (59.3)
Table 4 shows confidence-based co-decoding (AP+NN1) achieves highest F1 for Spanish (63.4) and Dutch (66.7); second-highest for German (63.7)
No analysis of why scheme selection differs between datasets or what properties determine optimal scheme
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Develop principled method for co-decoding scheme selection: (1) analyze properties of datasets where rank-based vs. confidence-based schemes perform better; (2) propose decision rule for selecting scheme based on dataset properties; (3) test decision rule on held-out datasets; (4) alternatively, develop meta-learning approach that learns optimal scheme per dataset.

concerns.title: Rank-based co-decoding heuristic not formally justified or optimized
concerns.description: Section 5 develops rank-based co-decoding that prioritizes annotation projection (high precision) and adds non-conflicting representation projection entities (balanced recall). This heuristic is based on observed precision-recall tradeoff but is not formally justified or optimized. No comparison with alternative prioritization schemes is provided.
evidence: Section 5 states: 'Based on this observation, we develop a rank-based co-decoding scheme that gives higher priority to the annotation projection system.'
Heuristic is based on observed precision-recall tradeoff (Section 5, Table 3) but not formally justified
No comparison with alternative schemes: (1) confidence-based weighting, (2) learned weights via logistic regression, (3) soft conflict resolution, (4) weighted combination of confidence scores
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compare alternative co-decoding schemes: (1) implement weighted combination of confidence scores from AP and RP; (2) learn weights via logistic regression on development set; (3) implement soft conflict resolution; (4) compare all schemes on development and test sets; (5) analyze which scheme performs best for different entity types, languages, or alignment qualities.

concerns.title: Conflict definition in co-decoding is binary without soft resolution or weighted combination
concerns.description: Footnote 3 defines conflict as binary: entities conflict if they have different boundaries but overlap, or same boundary but different tags. No soft conflict resolution or weighted combination is explored. This binary definition may be too strict and could miss opportunities to combine partial information from both systems.
evidence: Footnote 3 states: 'Two entities detected by two different systems conflict with each other if either 1) the two entities have different boundaries but overlap with each other; or 2) the two entities have the same boundary but different NER tags.'
Section 5 describes rank-based scheme: 'it will add all the entities detected by the representation projection system that do not conflict'
No discussion of soft conflict resolution (e.g., averaging confidence scores, weighted combination, boundary adjustment)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explore soft conflict resolution: (1) implement weighted combination for conflicting entities; (2) implement boundary adjustment; (3) implement tag voting; (4) compare all schemes on development and test sets; (5) analyze impact of conflict resolution strategy on precision, recall, and F1.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for F1 improvements
concerns.description: Paper reports F1 scores without confidence intervals or significance tests. Test sets are relatively small (30K–70K tokens), which may have high variance in F1 scores. Improvements reported may not be statistically significant.
evidence: Tables 3 and 4 report F1 scores without confidence intervals or significance tests
Test sets are 30K–45K tokens for in-house data and 35K–70K tokens for CoNLL data; relatively small for reliable F1 estimation
No discussion of variance in F1 scores or robustness to test set variation
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide statistical analysis: (1) compute 95% confidence intervals for F1 scores using bootstrap resampling; (2) conduct significance tests (e.g., McNemar's test) comparing co-decoding with individual systems; (3) report p-values for claimed improvements; (4) analyze variance in F1 across different test set samples.

concerns.title: Table 5 (comparison with prior work) is referenced but not provided; claims cannot be verified
concerns.description: Section 6.3 and Introduction reference Table 5 comparing proposed systems with Täckström et al. (2012) and Tsai et al. (2016) on CoNLL test data. However, Table 5 is not provided in the manuscript excerpt. Specific F1 scores, margins of improvement, and statistical significance cannot be verified.
evidence: Section 6.3 states: 'In Table 5 we compare our top systems (confidence or rank-based co-decoding of AP and NN1, determined by the development data) with the best results of the cross-lingual NER approaches proposed in Täckström et al. (2012) and Tsai et al. (2016) on the CoNLL test data.'

Introduction (lines 196–199) claims: 'The results show that the combined systems outperform the state-of-the-art cross-lingual NER approaches proposed in Täckström et al. (2012) and Tsai et al. (2016) on the CoNLL NER test data'
Table 5 is not provided in manuscript excerpt; cannot verify claims
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide Table 5 in manuscript with: (1) F1 scores for proposed systems and prior work on CoNLL test data; (2) margins of improvement (absolute and relative); (3) statistical significance tests comparing proposed systems with prior work; (4) error analysis comparing failure modes of proposed vs. prior systems.

concerns.title: Supervised baselines use different model architectures and training data sizes; fair comparison unclear
concerns.description: Section 6.2 and 6.3 compare weakly supervised systems with supervised baselines. However, supervised baselines use different model architectures and different training data sizes (90K–272K tokens). Fair comparison requires controlling for these factors.
evidence: Section 6.2 states: 'For the annotation projection approach, the source (English) NER system is a linear-chain CRF model trained with 320K tokens... and the target-language NER system is a 2nd-order MEMM model trained with 691K, 246K, 3.37M and 1.46M tokens of projection-labeled data'
Section 6.2 states: 'For representation projection, the source (English) NER systems are neural network models with architectures NN1 and NN2'
Table 3 shows supervised baselines trained on different data sizes: Japanese 272K, Korean 90K, German 125K, Portuguese 173K
No analysis of how F1 scales with training data size
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct fair comparison with supervised baselines: (1) train supervised baselines with same model architectures as weakly supervised systems; (2) train supervised baselines with same training data sizes as weakly supervised systems; (3) plot F1 as function of training data size for both weakly supervised and supervised approaches; (4) analyze gap between weakly supervised and supervised as function of data size.

concerns.title: Embedding dimensionality differs between source (300) and target (800) without justification
concerns.description: Section 4.1 specifies 300-dimensional embeddings for English and 800-dimensional embeddings for target languages. No justification for this choice is provided, and impact on mapping quality is not analyzed.
evidence: Section 4.1 states: 'We train 300-dimensional word embeddings for English. Following (Mikolov et al., 2013b), we use larger dimensional embeddings for the target languages, namely 800.'
No analysis of why 300 vs. 800 dimensions are chosen
No ablation study showing impact of embedding dimensionality on mapping quality or NER performance
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze embedding dimensionality: (1) test alternative dimensionalities (e.g., 300 for both, 600 for both); (2) measure mapping quality for each dimensionality choice; (3) measure NER F1 for each dimensionality choice; (4) provide justification for chosen dimensionalities.

concerns.title: Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) handling strategy impact not quantified
concerns.description: Section 4.3 describes OOV handling but impact of OOV handling on performance is not quantified. OOV rate and error contribution are not analyzed.
evidence: Section 4.3 states: 'Words which are not in the target vocabulary are projected into their English embeddings if found in the English vocabulary, or into an NER-trained unk vector otherwise.'
No analysis of OOV rate in target-language test sets
No comparison of OOV handling strategies
No analysis of how OOV handling affects precision, recall, and F1
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze OOV handling: (1) measure OOV rate in target-language test sets; (2) compare OOV handling strategies; (3) measure NER performance on OOV vs. in-vocabulary words; (4) analyze which entity types are affected by OOV.

alternative_interpretations: Frequency-based data selection may work not because English NER and alignment errors are independent, but because frequency-based filtering removes low-confidence projections regardless of error source. Alternative explanation: filtering removes entities with conflicting labels across multiple alignments, which may indicate ambiguous or difficult cases rather than independent errors.

Precision-recall tradeoff between AP and RP may reflect model architecture (MEMM for AP, neural network for RP) rather than projection approach. Alternative explanation: MEMM's locally-normalized model favors high-precision predictions, while neural network's global normalization enables more balanced precision-recall.

Co-decoding improvements may reflect complementarity of MEMM and neural network models rather than complementarity of annotation and representation projection approaches. Alternative explanation: combining two different model architectures (MEMM + NN) is inherently beneficial for ensemble methods.

Linear embedding mapping may work well not because embedding spaces have linear structure, but because linear mapping is robust to noise and overfitting compared to more complex non-linear mappings. Alternative explanation: simplicity of linear mapping prevents overfitting to small training dictionaries.

Data selection improvements may be driven by training data size reduction rather than quality improvement. Alternative explanation: smaller training sets (691K→5.10M for Japanese) may reduce overfitting and improve generalization, independent of label quality.

Rank-based co-decoding may outperform confidence-based co-decoding not because AP has higher precision, but because rank-based scheme is more robust to miscalibrated confidence scores from weakly-trained systems. Alternative explanation: confidence scores from weakly-trained systems may not be reliable, making confidence-based combination ineffective.
